content: During follow-up evaluations for laryngeal cancer, a rigid telescope, transnasal video, or fiberoptic endoscopy should be employed for laryngeal inspection, and the neck should be palpated to assess for abnormalities. Research indicates that laryngoscopy and stroboscopy are significantly more accurate (100% accuracy for both methods) compared to history-taking and physical examination alone (33% accuracy). The use of a videostroboscope provides additional valuable diagnostic information. Chest radiography is routinely performed during head and neck cancer follow-up to detect lung metastases and secondary primary tumors in the lung. However, studies suggest that annual chest radiographs are most beneficial for patients with laryngeal index tumors, as the incidence of secondary primary and metastatic tumors is higher in supraglottic cancer compared to glottic cancer. For patients with advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), chest CT is recommended over chest radiography for screening. Ultrasound (US) and US-guided fine needle aspiration cytology are critical tools for detecting cervical lymph node recurrences. Baseline CT or MRI imaging conducted 3 to 6 months after surgical, radiological, or combined treatment for high-risk head and neck cancer can be compared with subsequent imaging to detect abnormalities earlier. Patients treated with radiotherapy for laryngeal cancer require close follow-up, including clinical examinations and CT imaging every 3 to 4 months for the first 2 years post-treatment. MRI and PET-CT scans are superior for detecting recurrences and secondary primary tumors. PET-CT is particularly advantageous for systematic evaluation, with a reported sensitivity of 92% for detecting recurrent laryngeal cancer and nearly 100% accuracy in diagnosing distant metastases. In patients treated with primary radiation therapy alone, CT, MRI, and US cannot reliably differentiate post-radiation edema from recurrence. Therefore, baseline imaging with CT, MRI, or PET-CT should be performed 3 to 6 months after treatment for future reference. Patients undergoing transoral laser surgery for extended resection require regular laryngeal examinations every 4 to 8 weeks during the first year post-surgery due to the high risk of locoregional recurrence. Second-look microlaryngoscopy remains somewhat controversial but may be considered in cases of uncertain surgical margins, granulation tissue, web formation, or other abnormal tissue growth at the primary resection site. For patients who have undergone open partial laryngectomy, clinical laryngoscopic examination and CT imaging of the primary site are recommended. The optimal follow-up regimen after total or pharyngolaryngectomy is debated, but clinical examination of the remaining upper aerodigestive tract and neck should be performed, followed by contrast-enhanced CT if abnormalities are detected. PET-CT has been incorporated into follow-up protocols to screen for metastases in patients who have undergone surgery with adjuvant radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy. Patients treated with definitive chemoradiotherapy should undergo PET-CT at 3 months post-therapy to assess disease response and plan salvage neck surgery if necessary. Narrow-band imaging (NBI), which detects pathognomonic neoangiogenic patterns, has an 18% higher true-positive detection rate for laryngeal cancer lesions compared to conventional white-light endoscopy. NBI also demonstrates high accuracy and can differentiate abnormal regions from post-radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy inflammatory and/or cicatricial changes. Thyroid function evaluation is recommended for patients with laryngeal cancer who have undergone head and neck radiation therapy or thyroid gland removal. Thyroid function should be assessed twice yearly for the first 5 years post-treatment and annually thereafter. Radiation therapy to the head and neck results in biochemical hypothyroidism in at least 50% of patients, and partial or total thyroidectomy increases the risk of hypothyroidism. Thyroid dysfunction is determined by measuring serum levels of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and free thyroxine (FT4). Thyroid function is classified as euthyroidism (normal TSH and FT4), subclinical hypothyroidism (elevated TSH with normal FT4), or clinical hypothyroidism (elevated TSH with decreased FT4). Regular thyroid evaluations are recommended for at least 10 years post-treatment. Salvage surgery is recommended for recurrent laryngeal cancer after non-surgical treatment. Total laryngectomy is advised for recurrent T3/T4 cancer, while transoral laser microsurgery may be an option for recurrent T1/T2 cancer. Open partial laryngectomy, particularly supracricoid laryngectomy, can be considered for recurrent T2 and selected T3 cancers. The use of a pectoralis major muscle flap may reduce fistula formation after salvage total laryngectomy, but evidence is insufficient to recommend its routine use. Elective neck dissection is generally recommended for salvage treatment of supraglottic or transglottic cancer due to the high rate of occult metastasis. Ipsilateral elective neck dissection is advised for recurrent supraglottic, transglottic, or rT3/rT4 glottic cancer. Bilateral elective neck dissection may be considered for recurrent supraglottic cancer. Observation of the neck may be appropriate for some patients with rT1 or rT2 and clinically rN0 disease. For stomal recurrence after total laryngectomy, extensive resection is recommended in eligible cases. Risk factors for stomal recurrence include preoperative tracheostomy, subglottic involvement, advanced tumor stage, and paratracheal node metastasis. Radiotherapy and chemotherapy provide limited palliation, while extensive resection offers the best chance of cure.
